source.title: Explaining Grokking in Transformers through the Lens of Inductive Bias
source.authors: Jaisidh Singh; Diganta Misra; Antonio Orvieto

record.tranche_reason: Tests grokking on modular addition and uses architectural, optimization, and feature-measurement analyses to examine its timing and progress measures; it is not an explicit replication of the original method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own grokking, Fourier-structure, and feature-compressibility results. Values in the relevant figures are not transcribed numerically in the text, so figure-only values are recorded as such. Citations to other studies are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study reproduces grokking on modular addition (p=113, 30% train split) in one-layer transformers. It measures Fourier concentration and feature compressibility as progress measures across LayerNorm and optimizer modulators. It also gives results and an argument that the lazy-to-rich (readout-scale) account of V3 is confounded in this AdamW/cross-entropy setting. Because of that argument against a version it is T5, not just T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LN position and optimization choices (learning rate, weight decay, readout scale and softmax temperature) modulate grokking speed. They attribute the LN effect to MLP-input scale shortcuts and attention entropy. They find readout scale confounded as a laziness control under AdamW. Features evolve continuously, so grokking here is more than a lazy-to-rich transition. Feature compressibility offers a plausibly setting-agnostic progress measure.
record.recipe_differences: Uses modular addition and a transformer grokking setup, following the cited mechanistic-transformer setting; adds LayerNorm-position and optimization/readout-scale interventions and feature-compressibility measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Grokking speed varies with LayerNorm position, learning rate, weight decay, and readout scale. Readout-scale effects differ depending on whether learning rate is scaled as η0/α² or kept at η0.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing scale from the MLP input (SR-train) raises train loss far above default. SR-train rises during memorization and falls as the network groks; Av suppresses the rise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorization in grokking transformers relies on an MLP-input activation-scale shortcut that is abandoned at generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: LN on query/key inputs lowers attention-score entropy, and that configuration fails to generalize within 10k epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low attention entropy from normalizing query/key inputs impairs modular-addition generalization.

record.problems: Evidence is restricted to toy modular addition with transformers and adaptive optimization. Most curves are figure-only in the supplied text; results are often aggregated over 5 seeds, but no error bars or other uncertainty estimates are stated. Training-set size is not varied for the V1 claim.
record.rows_left_out: No applicable reported result was omitted.

untested.parts: Training-set size is fixed at 30%, so 'delay grows as the training set shrinks' is untested. Results are reported as test loss, not accuracy from chance.
Removal of memorizing components is not measured. Evidence that the measures anticipate the jump is mostly cross-configuration ordering, not within-run lead time.
Non-algorithmic data (images, text, molecules) is not tested. Initialization scale and weight norm are not used as on/off switches; only readout scale is tested.
Entirely untested; no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
Untested: circuit efficiency comparisons, a critical dataset size, and ungrokking.
Not tested as such. The authors say all LN variants reach periodic Fourier embeddings, but embedding Fourier concentration cannot tell clock from pizza algorithms.
Slingshots are noted, but optimizer and floating-point artifacts are not controlled or tested.

missing.what: Weight-decay sweep effects on effective rank and power-law α: higher λ gives more compressibility, earlier.
RMSNorm in place of LayerNorm gives very similar grokking modulation.
3-layer transformers (width 64) show grokking behavior very similar to one-layer models, with more slingshots.
Embeddings in all LN configurations reach periodic Fourier structure (CFourier ≥1.0).

record.verdict_notes: The training-set split is fixed at 30%, so V1's data-size dependence is untested. The values are figure-only with no error bars. The V3 challenge is limited to the readout-scale control in an AdamW/cross-entropy transformer setting; the authors restrict their claims to this scope. The V5 link rests only on the faster grokking seen with higher weight decay.

versions.untested_parts: Does not vary training-set size, report test accuracy as the metric, or establish that smaller training sets require more optimization.
Measures gradual Fourier structure and feature-compressibility trends, but does not measure memorizing components being removed later.
Does not test non-algorithmic data or initialization scale/weight norm as a lazy-to-rich switch.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
Although weight decay is varied, the study does not test whether an efficient circuit beats memorization or whether there is a critical dataset size or ungrokking.
Does not compare identifiable algorithms learned across runs.
Does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax artifacts disappearing under controls.

rows.subject: one-layer transformer
rows.size_stated: width 128; MLP hidden dimension 512; 4 attention heads
rows.operation_detail: Vary weight decay while holding learning rate fixed.
rows.value: Higher weight decay strengths lead to faster generalization and lower grokking
rows.note: The specific weight-decay values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Higher weight decay speeds grokking (Fig 4c) and increases compressibility (Fig 9). This is the direction V5's low-norm bias predicts, so the row also bears on V5.

rows.subject: one-layer transformer
rows.size_stated: width 128; MLP hidden dimension 512; 4 attention heads
rows.operation_detail: Vary readout scale α while scaling learning rate as η=η0/α².
rows.value: Higher readout scale leads to slower grokking
rows.note: The authors attribute this comparison to confounded learning rate, weight decay, and parameter-update norms.
rows.check: Higher readout scale delays grokking only under η0/α² scaling. The authors show this confounds learning rate, weight decay and update norms (Fig 5b), so it bears on V3's lazy-to-rich control.

rows.subject: one-layer transformer
rows.size_stated: width 128; MLP hidden dimension 512; 4 attention heads
rows.operation_detail: Vary readout scale α while keeping learning rate at η0=0.001.
rows.value: With constant learning rate, higher α generalizes faster
rows.note: The text says the trend is opposite to the η0/α² comparison and relates α to softmax temperature.
rows.check: For V1 grokking still occurs (observed). For V3, with constant learning rate and comparable update norms, higher readout scale (the 'lazier' setting) generalizes faster, the opposite of the lazy-to-rich prediction. The state given is for V3.

source_check.correct: V1: observed delayed generalization. V3: reversed readout-scale trend; higher α generalizes faster at learning rate 0.001, with comparable update norms in the initial training stage.
source_check.problem: The single reversed state fits the V3 scale prediction but incorrectly describes the linked V1 result.
